> AquaTrident, as its name suggests, is an aquaculture control/feedback system that monitors vital aquatic parameters, such as pH, Turbidity and TDS, designed for monitoring and regulating the environment conditions to be adequate for marine life specific types, in addition to providing real life data of the controlled system.

### 2026-10-11 – Schematic Designing:

**6h**

Schematic Designing:
I worked on designed the schematic on KiCad, I faced a lot of obstacles since it was kind of my first time to design a schematic in my life, so I recommend watching tutorials before you start your own schematic. And here is how my first designing session ended:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/b402d7ec15fadbd1be8b2ddb86896eed4f26627667d86f3dcd079bad7fe148ce.png)
Where I placed the main Arduino board, searched for the relay module and used the one in the image, placed 3 relay modules, and finally I placed 3 2x Pins to represent the actuators VCC & GND.

and then when I wanted to connect theses actuators to the relays, I got confused because of the relays, since their pins are labeled in number instead of actual labels (e.g. COM, IN, VCC, GND, NO, NC), so these connections need some research and understanding, which I am willing to do on the next working session.

Completing the Schematic:
I worked on solving the relay confusion and finally reached the solution and even understood the mechanism of how relays work, so here is how my schematic looked like after that designing session:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/551cb080f51294d7c11a71806e410faabb5ba6050c49e6c907bc7a97d4a41247.png)
So here is how it went:

Relay modules’ A2 pins were connected to Arduino’s digital pins (D5, D6, D7) along with connecting A1 pins to Arduino’s 5V and connecting all NO pins to actuators positive pins enabling control.

All relay’s COM (common) pins were connected to the 12V power supply and finally a common ground was established across all the circuit ensuring a stable and safe circuit.

I finally Finished the Schematic (:
I worked on completing the schematic, and polishing it until it reached this pretty design:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/04dfedab0e4d6748ed65ccdd16e41765e72605f796e8f90bb53770016c002d9b.png)

Placed 2x pins to represent the sensors wires.
Sensors’ signal pins were connected to Arduino’s analog pins (A0, A1, A2) enabling real time monitoring, sensors VCC pins were connected to Arduino’s 5V providing safe operating voltage, and LCD were attached to the Arduino through I2C enabling data logging.

You might take a closer look here (:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/f94533f116be536a04b98a54cffe64ce34e0f34f81e4f77b67899fb88ffc5099.png)

and when I say polishing I mean solved the errors, organized all the wire connections to look that pretty, established the GND & Power flags and blocked (X) all the pins that I didn't need.

Although connections wasn't easy and costed me a lot of time learning and wiring them, it weren't the final obstcale in the design, just as any IDE has a checking tool, KiCad has the ERC tool, so when I used this tool, more than 10 errors popped up across the design, however I debugged them untill I reached this:

### 2026-10-11 – pH Calibration

**6h**

pH Calibration
Aug 6, 2026, 1:07 AM
Omar Ezzat
We calibrated the sensors:
I searched and found out how to calibrate these sensors.

Two main calibration procedures were followed inside school chemistry lab:

A. Multipoint (3-point): this method was used to calibrate the pH sensor, where voltage was measured at 3 various standard buffer solutions (4,7,10).

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/8cbbdd3edea122c52584da2ff7b9d4dc73142706edf0a116d8798a09f25c99f3.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/ff260f623d9272eaef2782d7ad12376f4de0510f6e56ea3b604b90b4d10838c5.png)

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/3f2e399c9852438cea9eaa5720d7910e96cfab5a8a5717b90bfa17e2fbf72fef.png)

So the reason I struggled with calibrating the pH sensor was that I needed 3 standard buffer solutions as I mentioned before, but my school only had the 4pH solution, and I had distilled water, meaning the alkli or the low acidity solution (10 pH) was missing, as a result I tried to calibrate only using them, I made progress but the sensor wasn't accurate as it should be, however solutions are expensive and I couldn't afford them as they are sold as whole containers.

Each sensor took nearly 2 days of work, however if the sensors are purchased from a trusted place, if solutions where fresh and you used the right calibration methods you won't struggle as I did.

and that is a video that shows us calibrating the pH sensor:

TDS & Turbidity Calibration
Aug 6, 2026, 1:12 AM
We calibrated TDS & Turbidity sensors:
Second Calibration method:
B. Zero and Span: this method was used to calibrate the TDS and Turbidity sensors, where voltage was measured at (0 ppm) and (0 NTU) respectively then at (1000 ppm) and (3000 NTU) respectively. Mapping output voltage to standard values, calibration curves were generated at Excel, driving equations that are used in code to convert raw voltage into real accurate measurements, as shown in this pic.:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/vo5InRJ1b7jDKxSNMRH4a83w3DzOrroc/2d8a1e5f0c6fdfecb4cd1f6e2f11464b5ff91a4e0294ee43e5300adba3c41c7e.png)

a part of the TDS code.

we also developed with the help of AI a function to get the medium readings of a sensor so it is clearer and more accurate, as can be seen in this screenshot:
